ai.seo_question: Why is the Prophet's poverty considered a sign of divine honour rather than humiliation?
ai.summary: Sharif al-Radi presents this rhetorical argument to reframe asceticism (zuhd) not as a deprivation but as a distinct mark of divine favor, contrasting the Prophet's restrained worldly life with the lavish provision granted to others. This perspective is central to Shia theological discourse, emphasizing that spiritual proximity to God often necessitates a detachment from material excess, thereby validating the Imams' own modest lifestyles as imitations of the Prophet. The passage invites the reader to use reason ('aql) to discern that true honor lies in spiritual purity rather than worldly accumulation.

en.sayed-ali-raza: Certainly there was in the Prophet of Allāh all that would apprise you of the evils of this world and its defects,
namely that he remained hungry along with his chief companions, and despite his great nearness the allurements of the world remained remote from him.
Now, one should see with one’s intelligence whether Allāh honoured Muḥammad — the peace and blessings of Allāh be upon him and his descendants — as a result of this or disgraced him.
If he says that Allāh disgraced him, he certainly lies and perpetrates a great untruth. If he says Allāh honoured him,
he should know that Allāh dishonoured the others when He extended the (benefits of the) world for him but held them away from him who was the nearest to Him of all men.
